clue.text: See 7
Accommodation (not hotel) for more than one banker

indicators.note: 'not hotel' says the hotel letter is to be left out of the accommodation word

parts.note: a house is accommodation
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is told there is lodging without a hotel for a group of bankers.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'banker' is crossword slang for a river (it has banks); several English rivers are called the Ouse, hence 'more than one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain has several rivers bearing this name, in Yorkshire, Sussex and East Anglia, so it names more than one river.

clue.text: Anne who hosts with Nick like this in pub?

parts.note: to nick is to steal, to rob

indicators.note: 'in pub' places the phrase for 'like this' within the word for a pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
so means in this way, like this

explanation.surface: A question about a TV presenter co-hosting with Nick, the way people do in a pub quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a presenter's first name (Nick Robinson hosts BBC Radio 4's Today) but is the verb for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Robinson is the British TV presenter who hosted The Weakest Link and Countdown.

clue.text: Now has a tenant — start to search for keys

parts.note: a property that now has a tenant is let, so 'is let'

indicators.note: the start of the word search gives its first letter

explanation.surface: A landlord, having found a tenant, starts hunting for the house keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keys' looks like door keys, but a key (or cay) is a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Keys are small low islands, especially coral ones, which is what islets are.

clue.text: Directions for securing empty life raft

indicators.note: the directions hold the other letters, securing them between them

parts.note: S and W are the compass directions south and west

indicators.note: an empty word loses its inside, leaving just the outer letters of life

explanation.surface: Instructions for tying down an empty life raft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raft' looks like the boat, but it means a large quantity, as does a slew.
explanation.definitionFit: A raft of things and a slew of things are both informal words for a large number.

clue.text: Some, originally offensive, don't change

indicators.note: originally points at the opening letter of the word Some

parts.note: the Tet Offensive was the 1968 Vietnam War campaign, so offensive can call up Tet

explanation.surface: An editor notes that some words, though offensive at first, should be left alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offensive' reads as rude, but it is the noun for a military campaign, here the Tet Offensive of the Vietnam War.
explanation.definitionFit: Stet is the proofreader's instruction meaning let the original text stand, reversing a marked correction.

clue.text: Surprisingly short Lord Sugar keeps you talking a lot

indicators.note: the shuffled letters keep the 'you' letter held within them
surprisingly signals the letters turn up in an unexpected order
a short word is cut off before its end, losing the last letter of Lord

parts.note: U sounds like you, as in text speak

explanation.surface: Lord Sugar, the businessman from The Apprentice, is pictured as unexpectedly brief yet keeping you chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short Lord' gives LOR; with SUGAR rearranged that makes GARRULOS, and U slips in near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A garrulous person is excessively talkative, chattering on at length.

clue.text: Regarding bed hopping, crossing capital abandoned

indicators.note: hopping suggests the letters jump about into a new order

explanation.surface: Something about bed-hopping, with a capital city crossing given up on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed hopping' reads as infidelity, but 'hopping' is the anagram signal for REGARDING BED.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden Bridge was a planted pedestrian bridge proposed across the Thames in London, cancelled in 2017 after heavy public spending.

clue.text: Delayed restrictions of movement — clown does talk rubbish

indicators.note: talking rubbish is talking nonsense, so the letters are made into a jumble

explanation.surface: A clown talks nonsense about late curbs on movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'clown' doubles as a political jibe in this pandemic-themed puzzle; 'rubbish' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockdowns were Covid-era restrictions on people's movement; ones imposed too late are delayed.

clue.text: Get flat denial, occasionally backtracking

indicators.note: backtracking means going back the way you came, so the letters run right to left
occasionally means now and then, taking every other letter of denial

explanation.surface: Someone gets a flat refusal now and then, followed by a retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' takes E, I, L from denial; 'backtracking' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie is to assume a horizontal position, which is to get flat.

clue.text: Start of poorly-paid job for one of the plebs

indicators.note: the start of the word poorly-paid is its first letter

parts.note: a role is a job or function

explanation.surface: A badly paid first job for an ordinary worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Prole, from proletarian, is a disparaging term for a working-class person, a pleb.

clue.text: Free — good choice to go over part of roof

parts.note: to rid is to free

indicators.note: going over is turning back on itself, so the word for choice is read backwards

parts.note: elite as an adjective means choice, select

explanation.surface: Free advice that a good option is to recover part of the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go over' reverses ELITE into ETILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge tile is one of the curved tiles capping the apex line of a pitched roof.

clue.text: Now recants? An amazingly ineffective (and costly) method of crowd control

definitions.text: ineffective (and costly) method of crowd control

indicators.note: something done amazingly is done astonishingly, so the letters come out in a surprising order

explanation.surface: Someone backtracks on a pricey and useless way of controlling crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: London bought water cannon in 2014 for over £300,000; their use was never licensed and they were sold for scrap, hence 'ineffective (and costly)'.
explanation.definitionFit: Water cannons are vehicle-mounted high-pressure hoses used by police to disperse crowds.

clue.text: Laments on independence — look around outside

indicators.note: outside places the turned-round 'look' word around the others
around means turned about, so the word for look is read backwards

parts.note: to see is to look
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side
I is the abbreviation for independent or independence

explanation.surface: Mournful songs about independence, urging people to look about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is the cricket term: the on side is also called the leg side. 'around' reverses the look word and 'outside' wraps it round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem or song, a lament, often for the dead.

clue.text: Keen on accepting right opening

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: into means keen on, as in being into music

explanation.surface: Someone eager to take the correct opportunity.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro, short for introduction, is the opening part of a song or speech.

clue.text: What's afoot? Conservative leader involved in misconduct?

indicators.note: involved in means caught up within, so a letter is placed inside the footwear word

parts.note: a sandal is something worn on the foot

indicators.note: the leader of the word Conservative is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Asking what's going on: is a Conservative party leader caught up in wrongdoing?
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's afoot?' reads as what's happening, but it means something on a foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal is a disgraceful act or wrongdoing causing public outrage.

clue.text: Tip off old prince — essentially FBI's given up

indicators.note: given up means abandoned, so a letter is taken out of the prince's name

parts.note: Albert was Queen Victoria's consort, Prince Albert

indicators.note: essentially means at its core, taking the central letter of FBI

explanation.surface: Someone warns an aging royal that the FBI has abandoned a case.
explanation.walkthrough: The core of FBI is B, removed from ALBERT.
explanation.definitionFit: To alert someone is to warn them, to tip them off.

clue.text: Welshman from Snowdonia done over

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the concealed letters read backwards
from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A Welshman from the mountains of Snowdonia has been beaten up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'done over' reads as beaten up; 'done' supplies letters and 'over' reverses them.
explanation.definitionFit: Dai, a short form of David, is a stock Welsh first name, standing for a typical Welshman.

clue.text: Accomplishment achieving nothing extra for the most part (I bend being flexible)

parts.note: getting means achieving, as in getting results

indicators.note: being flexible means bending into other shapes, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: for the most part means most of the word, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A sardonic remark: something hailed as an achievement that mostly gains nothing extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the most part' trims EXTRA to EXTR; with O, I and BEND that is rearranged into BREXIT DONE. 'Get Brexit Done' was the Conservatives' 2019 election slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting Brexit done was trumpeted as the government's great achievement, so it is presented as an accomplishment.

clue.text: In French describing old age

indicators.note: describing in its sense of drawing round, so the French word encloses a letter

parts.note: en is French for in

explanation.surface: A phrase in French that describes old age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is used in its geometric sense of tracing round something.
explanation.definitionFit: An eon is an immensely long period of time, an age.

clue.text: Sibling repaired chain and inner tubes

parts.note: bro is short for brother, a sibling

indicators.note: repaired means put back together, here in a different order

explanation.surface: A brother fixes a bicycle chain and some inner tubes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inner tubes' looks like bike parts, but means air passages inside the body.
explanation.definitionFit: The bronchia are the branching air tubes within the lungs, inner tubes of the body.

clue.text: Head of state tending to alarm

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: care is tending, looking after

explanation.surface: A head of state inclined to cause panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' looks like a president but just gives S; 'tending to' reads as 'inclined to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scare is a sudden fright, an alarm, and to scare is to alarm.

clue.text: Once the greatest issue for her

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the late boxer, called himself The Greatest
issue means offspring, such as a son

explanation.surface: A once-supreme concern that matters most for a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Alison is a woman's first name, so 'her' stands for it as any girl's name would.

clue.text: See 12
Cheers with a bit of speculation — figure buffoon's heading for exit?

indicators.note: a bit of the word speculation here is its first letter
heading for exit means the letter is leaving the shape word

parts.note: an oblong is a geometric figure, a rectangle

indicators.note: the heading of buffoon's is its first letter

explanation.surface: Goodbye, with a guess that a clownish figure is heading out the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is British for goodbye as well as thanks. 'buffoon' hints at the then prime minister, Boris Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: So long is an informal farewell, like the British parting 'cheers'.

clue.text: Now happening to bring work forward? Such an illusion!

indicators.note: to bring something somewhere is to carry it to a new place within the word
forward says the piece goes to the front of the word, earlier than before

parts.note: topical means relating to current events
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A manager is told to bring a deadline forward, and it proves illusory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bring forward' takes OP from TOPICAL and puts it at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An optical illusion is a trick of vision, so 'such an illusion' names that kind.

clue.text: Reluctant to admit it hurt Britain — rogue

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the outer word takes the others inside

parts.note: coy means shy, reluctant
ow is the cry when something hurts

explanation.surface: A rogue who won't confess to having damaged Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: A cowboy in British usage is a dishonest or unqualified tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a cowboy is an unscrupulous trader or operator, a rogue.

clue.text: Restrictions abandoned too early, doctors initially considered

indicators.note: initially points at the first letter of each of the preceding words

explanation.surface: Doctors' first verdict was that the restrictions were dropped too soon.
explanation.definitionFit: To be rated is to be judged or considered, as in rated a success.

clue.text: Unlikely score, 80%

indicators.note: 80% of a five-letter word is its first four letters, so the end is dropped

parts.note: a tally is a score or running count

explanation.surface: An improbable result: a score of eighty per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: A tall story is an unlikely one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall means hard to believe, as in a tall tale or tall order.

clue.text: See 18
See 8
Record is kept by spurned former adviser initially

indicators.note: kept by means held inside, so the initials hold the other letters

parts.note: Dominic Cummings, Boris Johnson's ousted chief adviser, has the initials D and C

explanation.surface: A record is held by a discarded ex-adviser's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a gramophone record or other recording medium.

clue.text: I'm surprised — two holiday houses!

indicators.note: houses is a verb here, meaning the words contain the answer

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at owning two holiday homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' reads as a noun but is a verb for containing.
explanation.definitionFit: Oho is an exclamation of surprise or triumph.

clue.text: Obvious — doesn't have one idea

indicators.note: doesn't have means lacks, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: plain means obvious
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: It's clear: someone lacks a single idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan is a scheme or intention, an idea of what to do.

clue.text: Makes secure from wind (also building at back of garden)

indicators.note: building means assembling, so these letters are put together afresh
the back of the word garden is its final letter

explanation.surface: Fixing something down against the wind, with a new building at the end of a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: To nail something down is to fasten or settle it firmly, to secure it.
